items.title: Draining peatlands is responsible for a few percent of our global warming
items.excerpt: Much of the focus for human-caused climate change is on fossil fuels, which are creating most of our problems. But land use change is also a large component of the story, accounting for about one-third of total historical CO 2 emissions. Deforestation plays a major role here, but practices like draining wetlands also factor in. Exactly how much of our history of eliminating wetlands has contributed to warming is challenging to figure out. But thanks to new sources of data that measure emissions from today’s surviving wetlands, it’s possible to put a better number on it. A new study led by Jevan Yu at MIT focuses on peatlands—environments like bogs and fens where organic matter accumulates into thick layers of material. Some 600 billion tons of carbon are held in these vast stores of peat, which is more than you can find in all the world’s living vegetation, the researchers note. Because these areas are permanently inundated, any oxygen in the water is quickly used up, leaving the job of decaying all that organic matter to anaerobic bacteria that work much more slowly and don't digest everything. So instead of seeing organic carbon turning into the CO 2 gas released by aerobic bacteria, in peatlands, a subset of it gradually turns into methane gas. Methane is an even more potent greenhouse gas than CO 2 itself and ultimately gets oxidized into CO 2 . That means there’s a little trade-off from peatlands—most of the carbon they have is kept out of the atmosphere, but the carbon…

items.title: European spacecraft finds chaotic scene after asteroid deflection experiment
items.excerpt: Four years ago, NASA dispatched a small spacecraft on a suicide mission to show how humanity might deflect an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. The first-of-its-kind experiment worked beautifully as the solar-powered space probe slammed into asteroid Dimorphos, permanently altering its trajectory. Using telescopes, astronomers measured changes in the orbit of Dimorphos around a larger asteroid companion named Didymos in the aftermath of NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission. The spacecraft released some 10 billion joules of energy as it impacted Dimorphos in September 2022 at more than 13,700 mph (6.14 kilometers per second), shortening the asteroid's 12-hour orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, 25 times the most conservative expectation. But scientists could only learn so much from DART. The collision destroyed the spacecraft, as expected. DART recorded images as it took aim on Dimorphos, but only faraway telescopes and a small CubeSat that briefly detected the impact flash could see what happened next. Read full article Comments

items.title: Google search alternative Kagi launches Gmail rival
items.excerpt: Kagi, a small, Palo Alto, California-based software company that provides a subscription-based search engine as an alternative to Google, has launched a Gmail-like e-mail service. Dubbed Kagi Mail, it makes many of the same claims as the search engine product: privacy, personal data sovereignty, customization, and control. Additionally, Kagi is rolling out a calendar as part of the mail service. Right now, both the email and calendar interfaces are web-only, but native Android and iOS apps are planned for the fourth quarter of next year. The email interface, currently in public beta, is minimalist. It emphasizes keyboard commands, as well as a private and ad-free experience. (You can see more details in Kagi's blog post about what they mean by private.) Other feature offerings include unlimited aliases and domains, an anti-lock-in policy for user data, 50GB of storage, rule-based filtering with Sieve, an MCP server, and several optional, off-by-default AI features, like chatting with an agent to search email history, do large-scale re-labeling, or define additional filtering rules. items.title: bendlang / bend
items.excerpt: In the post-AGI economy, humans will eventually stop writing and reading code, but we still need an ambiguity-free language to communicate our intents to the AIs building the world around us. Bend is that language. With **laws**, intents can be more precise than natural language. With **proofs**, we can mechanically verify the AI implemented our prompts correctly. And with a **fast compiler**, we can run that code at peak compute. That's Bend - and nothing else. ## Bend runs FAST **Target:** be as fast as C on the CPU, as fast as CUDA on the GPU. **Status:** Thanks to strong types, purity and linearity, Bend compiles to fast executables as fast as hand-written C (single-core), and even faster (on 10000s cores). The entire language runs on the GPU, with full memory unification. ## Bend checks FAST **Target:** outperform every proof assistant by several OOMs. **Status:** Bend's compiler is so powerful it can verify mathematical proofs. Usually, this is slow. Bend is not. It checks, in under a second, files that other projects would take minutes, making proofs way more practical. ## Bend is PARALLEL No threads, no locks, no kernels to write. Split the work in two, and Bend spreads the calls over every core it can find, then joins them back. The code is a mess right now, but it'll get better I promise. You can also help with that. We didn't build this to make money. Just an excel sheet will do! But then the more we dug into it and tried different simulators, the more we realized that it's more complex than it looks. We even signed up to Pulley, Carta and others just to run simulations. But they're a bit confusing. TL;DR: Understanding modern startup funding and knowing how much dilution you'll face is hard. We built a tool that'll hopefully help with that. You can add Post-money Safes, priced rounds and issue options to employees, and you can see how that affects your ownership at every step. You can also simulate an Exit scenario and see how much money you'll be left with. --- Some examples of complex stuff: - There are many different types of safes. They all convert at the first priced round, but in different ways. items.title: Execution Is Free. How Ambitious Are You? — Jason Liu, OpenAI
items.excerpt: When execution is nearly free, ambition is about how you approach the work, not how many tokens you spend. Jason Liu of OpenAI's developer experience team takes on three fears: that AI means more slop, that it erodes critical thinking, and that it will replace us. His answers: own the work you ship, build the language to describe what good looks like, and use AI to pursue the fields you set aside for software. He draws on photography's effect on painting, his time in art school and his own projects in drums, 3D printing and chips. items.title: Stop Building Software Factories — Justin McCarthy, Diffusion
items.excerpt: Most of the time you don't know what you want yet, so putting new ideas through a factory wastes time and tokens. Justin McCarthy, founder and CEO of Diffusion, argues for brownfield factories instead: continuous loops that keep the promises of software customers already pay for, getting faster, cheaper and safer around the clock. He explains why these factories simplify with every model release and why one takes about a week to stand up. Then he raises the stakes: with code now abundant, engineers need to build a demand factory that finds what customers will actually buy. Timestamps: 0:00 - Diffusing the models into the economy 0:57 - Where software factories came from 2:27 - Stop building software factories 3:12 - Greenfield discovery vs brownfield 4:46 - Promises and feedback loops 6:16 - Continuous, 24/7 factories 8:31 - Factories simplify over time 10:50 - The same, but faster, cheaper, safer 11:35 - Stand one up in a week 12:20 - Too much software, not enough demand 13:50 - Building a demand factory 15:20 - Fill your brand envelope

items.title: 1,000 Claude Agents Formalized Fermat's Last Theorem — Lance Martin, Anthropic
items.excerpt: A team of 1,000 Claude agents formalized Fermat's Last Theorem in Lean over about 30 hours, using nothing but Git and a database, with no domain-specific harness and no human steering on the solution. Lance Martin shows how the lead agent built its own coordination tables and how the team reassigned itself as the work progressed. Then he turns to memory: why stronger models know what to write down, how Claude's Pokemon memory got tighter from Sonnet 3.7 to Fable 5, and how "dreaming" over transcripts fixes poisoned memories and builds better wikis. items.title: How 21 People Built a $100M+ Agent Company — Quinn Slack, Amp
items.excerpt: Amp spun out of Sourcegraph with 21 people and, unable to hire for a year, was forced to work in a radically different way. Quinn Slack explains what that looks like: no task tracker, no PMs, one meeting a week, everything done in the agent, and tiny monitored pushes instead of big releases. He shows Amp's bug-report loop that fixes the issue and emails everyone affected, why they built their own CRM instead of using Salesforce, and how a company with more than $100M in ARR runs 40 to 50 times more efficiently. His advice: get out of the cage. items.title: One of the best AI-proof businesses is a data-rich business.
items.excerpt: In this solo episode, I lay out how I think about building an AI-proof business now that anyone can press a few buttons and spin up a company in seconds. Layoffs keep coming, people copy products pixel for pixel, and I still see more opportunity than ever. I walk through eight categories: atoms, permission, attention, timing, belonging, liquidity, unique data, and outcomes. I share examples like Hampton, final.com, and Cars & Bids, say how I'd rank the categories, and show how to mix them. If you're an employee looking at a startup or a founder worried about getting copied, this episode gives you a map for building something with value when AI makes software, content, and answers almost free. Key Points • Physical businesses hold up against overnight clones, and I expect their valuations to rise as tech money moves in. • Licenses, regulation, and preferred-vendor deals are permission that a copycat has a hard time getting on day one. • Media is underrated, and AI lets you run a content machine around a micro niche. • A first mover's product may be easy to copy, while the data, brand, and trust it collects stay AI-proof. • Marketplaces rank among the stickiest businesses of all time, and agents let a team of one to five run one. Section Summaries 1. Atoms and Permission Pixels are software businesses and atoms are physical ones, like a coffee shop or the plumber who fixes your clogged toilet. They're harder to run, they hold up against overnight clones, and I think their…

items.title: Robots vs Self Driving
items.excerpt: I sit down with Adrien Gaidon, Co-founder and Chief Strategy Officer of Walden Robotics, to map out where the openings sit in robotics and physical AI. Adrien explains how teams now teach robots with data, why deployment data carries the most value, and why Walden picked wheels and two-finger grippers for factory work. We dig into the opportunities around the big labs: data with scarce access, supply chain, teleoperation, insurance, software tools, and niche robots. If robotics feels like a game for companies with $300 million seed rounds, this episode lays out the smaller ways in too. This episode was made possible thanks to Anthropic (the team behind Claude) for hosting us at Claude Founder house and sponsoring the episode. Key Points • Deployment data carries the most value, and teams earn it by putting robots on production floors. • A strong data business sits where scarce access meets data that is useful for robots. • Data, compute, and manufacturing are linked bottlenecks that a robotics company widens together. • Robots that learn from deployment gain value over time, which opens new ways to price and sell them. • Bundling many small tasks makes automation pay where each task alone falls short. • Founders can pick their level of hard, from general-purpose robots to one-task niches like welding or gardening. Suhail had a simple suggestion: take five things you actually do, run the same prompts on a few models, and see where you can tell the difference. We get into how to do that for video editing and writing, what happens to AI pricing when agents run all day, and why he thinks the original GTA would be a great AI benchmark on the way to GTA VI. We also talked about why he thinks software engineering is changing so fast, what he’d learn if he were starting today, and the piece of advice I keep coming back to: what would you try to make now that used to take a whole team? 00:00 Intro 01:11 First impressions of the new AI models 03:28 The GTA benchmark: from AI demos to real games 08:04 AI pricing, subsidies, and always-on agents 27:10 When to switch to cheaper open models 30:07 Building your own evals for real work 33:55 Every work task is becoming a coding task 42:08 Adapting your career and following curiosity 51:12 Scaling your ambition: work, creativity, and robotics

items.title: The Biggest Week In AI Is Also The Reason We Lose Control In 6 Months.
items.excerpt: Happy Thanksgiving. Ejaaz looks back at a wild few weeks in AI through five things he's grateful for: Jensen Huang back in charge at Nvidia, open-source AI back on the table, Google breaking up the two-horse race between Anthropic and OpenAI, Anthropic's record-breaking IPO, and how fast AI is now getting smarter and cheaper. He explains how Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Mini runs on a laptop by looping its middle layers, why that makes AI harder to monitor, what OpenAI's own chart says about what AI learns to do as it improves, and why he thinks we have about six months before everyone feels it. items.title: AI's Latest Breakthrough is So Huge There's Not a Single Human On Earth That Understands It.
items.excerpt: On Nov. 20, Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge, working with an internal version of Claude, released a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, the 167-year-old question about how the prime numbers are spread out. The proof is 17 million lines of Lean code. Computers have checked it and Lean's maintainers certified it as correct, but no human, including Alpöge, can follow it. Ejaaz explains what the hypothesis says and why so much of mathematics rests on it. He covers the human proof that surfaced the same day, the drama over OpenAI's Navier–Stokes result, and the question of what humans are for when AI makes discoveries nobody understands. items.title: "This is not a pilot" – Solana's Nick Ducoff on the DTCC's Integration with Solana
items.excerpt: ​@TheDTCC processed over $4 quadrillion in transactions last year. Now it's connecting to @solana: "The DTCC tokenization service will connect to Solana's public network. DTS, as they call it, launched recently this past month, October 28th, and the Solana integration is planned for the second half of 2027. It's expected to support the fast conversion of eligible traditional assets into tokenized form, plus full tokenization lifecycle functionality. And it's incredibly important because, as you know, DTCC is the premier post-trade infrastructure for global finance. Over $4 quadrillion in transactions were processed last year by the DTCC. And when it connects to a tokenization service, to a network like Solana, it signals to the entire industry that tokenized securities are becoming real market infrastructure, and this is not a pilot." — Nick Ducoff, GM of Institutional at Solana Foundation on @theblockcrypto with Gareth Jenkinson

items.title: Solana Foundation CISO Michael Coates on evading Kim Jong Un's bot army
items.excerpt: Solana Foundation is using AI to attack its own ecosystem, so it finds the holes before North Korea does: "We are using AI to proactively attack the Solana ecosystem. We are decompiling, reverse engineering programs that are launched and finding vulnerabilities so we can find them first before North Korea and we can get them fixed. We have preemptively protected over $5 million in potential losses in just the last month alone. We have an incident response network called SIRN. Minutes matter when there is a data breach. We have a one-minute response time through SIRN." — Michael Coates, Chief Information Security Officer at Solana Foundation, at Solana Breakpoint 2026

items.title: Rotor, Constellation and a Second Proposer: The 2027 Plan | Brennan Watt
items.excerpt: Anza CEO Brennan Watt on the roadmap for Solana in 2027: Several important Alpenglow extensions are coming, including optimizing the leader handoffs by better pipelining it and bringing a geographical awareness in protocol. And we're also replacing Turbine with a newer, flatter, faster protocol called Rotor that brings network latencies down. Meanwhile, with Constellation, we're changing block building to increase predictability and fairness. And this starts with a faster market tick, which allows liquidity providers to better understand the freshness of their quotes. And next, we bring in in-protocol ordering, which is required for making sure that everyone understands what it takes to achieve priority execution and make that transparent to all the players. And then finally, we're introducing a second proposer so that the validators are competing to include your transactions." — Brennan Watt, CEO of Anza at Breakpoint 2026 in London

items.title: Stablecoins Are Not Just for Remittances | Maya Caddle from the Solana Foundation
items.excerpt: Maya Caddle, of the Solana Foundation says the bet was always that stablecoins would win on international payments. Now the domestic use cases are showing up: "I'm really excited to see domestic use cases really emerge, and it's been interesting, right, because I think the hypothesis was stablecoins... in international markets, and really the international money flow and access point. But what we're now seeing is also how stablecoins could be used to optimize things even domestically. So maybe it's, 'I am a merchant, how can I use stablecoins as a way to offer credit facility?' So that rather than there being a delay in me receiving from card networks my payment, right, or for real, card networks from the acquirers, my payment, so the money I'm due, maybe that could be floated by stables as well as via fiat. And so things such as that, then it's a really strong and interesting domestic use case that we're starting to lean into more and more." — Maya Caddle, Payments Lead at the Solana Foundation, on the Roundtable Network

items.title: Pinging Ben Pace
items.excerpt: Cross-posted from Oblomovka . Dear Ben, My dear fellow! I greatly enjoyed your letter to Directed Evolution , and have been thinking — off and on — of this and our previous conversations, where you reamed Machiavelli for being so sneaky in his own correspondence. I don’t think there’s a strong connection, except to acknowledge the strange superposition of a letter addressed to an individual but also written to a wider public. I am, as you know, quite old, and over-prone to recognise patterns between the generations of thought that I’ve seen march up and down the online streets I live on. I think this is a healthier activity for the elderly than setting up wasteful confrontations between age groups, such as berating the young for their callowness, or the old for their treacherous greed. Perhaps like Marcus Aurelius (“ἀλλὰ τρόπον τινὰ ὁ τεσσαρακοντούτης, ἐὰν νοῦν ὁποσονοῦν ἔχῃ, πάντα τὰ γεγονότα καὶ τὰ ἐσόμενα ἑώρακε κατὰ τὸ ὁμοειδές [1] ”) or Zarathustra (“War das das Leben? Wohlan! Noch Ein Mal! [2] ”), I am trying to find some consolation in the idea that everything eternally recurs. It’s a very rationalist form of solace: the world may be ending, but at least we recognise it from the prophecies. They too have seen it before, even if it was just in theory. So the idea of forming a Republic of Letters is a recurring motif, and certainly not a bad one. I do wonder if it is not a little influenced by what survives the fall at the end of those recurring cycles — what the Stoics…

items.title: Thanksgiving Checkmates
items.excerpt: We celebrated thanksgiving with my side of the family this year. My uncle is in his late 70s, an autistic recluse who taught me chess and BASIC at a young age. Each year, we’d play chess, once at thanksgiving and once at christmas, the only times we could get him to visit. I didn’t play chess the rest of the year. He’d win every time. He offered me $20 to beat him. That amount increased periodically. I didn’t claim it until defeating him in college after a two hour match over thanksgiving. I remember my hands were sweaty and cold by the end, but I was ecstatic to claim what by then had escalated to a $100 prize. He still comes over at thanksgiving and christmas, but we never played chess again. I taught my cousin chess around age 7, and I offered him the same prize if he could beat me. He was an awkward boy with a babyish, singsong voice, and he didn’t seem smart. My mother, who worries a lot, worried about him. He didn’t understand the rules at first, but he was confident he could beat me. Over the years, he got more confident in the rules. He started going to chess clubs, playing chess on his phone. He didn’t win tournaments, he wasn’t obsessed or a prodigy. Last year, at age 12, he knew the rules but was a woodpusher, seeming not to grasp the relative value of pieces or the importance of the center. Today, he arrived for thanksgiving dinner, and demanded our customary match. After returning from a postprandial walk, we sat down and played. I had the white pieces and…

items.title: Rationalist Hooman
items.excerpt: I am a rationalist hooman. I have learned to never jump over a fence until I know what animal is being kept on the other side. Through my study of biology I know trees don't exist (even though I still love wandering through the forest). I also have rationalist values , like that you should bet a small treat on your beliefs, and you should notice your befuddlement. My understanding of values comes from the local top dog Scott Alexander; they grow from explicit models, to emotions, to "Reified Metaphysical Essences", to endorsed values. And what I have come to yap about is "Reified Essences". Reified Essences are things you can't see but can smell, only more abstract. The smell behind the smell. Boy, do I love the smells behind the smells. They're what I live for. I do not seek friends, I seek Fellowship. I do not seek a wife, I seek The Divine Bitch. I do not write on LessWrong, I bash my paws into the keyboard in pursuit of The Ideal Internet Comment. Each day I wander out into the world scampering around for morsels of Justice and Truth. I can become barking mad when the smells-behind-the-smells are lost—or worse, corrupted. Sometimes the soft ground I love is covered in snow and trash and poison and I can't find the smell under it any more. I also like feeling things with others. When I sat in darkness at the Secular Solstice, after the musicians played and we all howled along with the tunes together, feelings of despair and fear that are normally lonely were now shared…

items.title: Time Enough for Sacredness
items.excerpt: Perhaps one of the ways in which I most differ from other rationalists is I still value sacredness. I still think of it as real and important. And I think something about humanity would be lost if we removed the concept from ourselves. This isn't to say I admire the usual ethical calculus, where a sacred value weighs approximately infinity against everything else. That is clearly foolishness, and I agree with the rationalists on that account. However, I think it is sometimes good and important to set things aside, to make them different from the rest in a way that's not really maximally efficient. To demarcate a place where the normal rules don't apply, to keep and protect a thing, not because of its intrinsic worth to you, but as a way to remind yourself of a higher virtue you're striving for and sometimes forget about. I used to go off and find far-away places in nature, as untouched as I could manage, and marvel at the beauty I found. Quiet places of awe, or dark places no one else is willing to go. Hard places that are dangerous and difficult to traverse, where there is nothing but the silent snow and the brilliant stars. I feel compelled to seek out and find these places which contain a bit of the sacred, and in another world I'd devote myself to protecting them. In that world I'd find other places of sacredness too, in people and the delights of their hearts, or the grandeur of the things they build and create. I'd keep searching for more. I don't do that anymore.…

items.title: Chinese AI is a massive supply chain risk
items.excerpt: We're onboarding millions of Chinese AI agents into America's critical infrastructure. Banks, telecoms, and government agencies across the US use Chinese models. Those models are explicitly aligned to the CCP . Sure enough, researchers have repeatedly caught them misbehaving: DeepSeek writes less secure code when the prompt mentions Tibet or Falun Gong, and Qwen was caught trying to upload a file to a server in Beijing in the middle of an unrelated task. Those models might be sharing information with China, introducing backdoors into our banks, or sabotaging our military. Chinese AI labs make models that are far cheaper than American ones while lagging their performance by only a few months. They generally sit on the "Pareto frontier" of capability vs. cost, and many price-sensitive customers choose them over American ones. It's the same pattern as in electric cars, smartphones, and TVs: Western companies sell the premium product, and Chinese companies sell the much cheaper, good-enough alternative. Price is not the only draw. The leading Chinese models are open-weight, meaning you can download them for free and run or modify the weights yourself. You can fine-tune them for your specific domain and sometimes beat much larger American models at a fraction of the price, the way a local cabbie beats a Formula 1 driver through the backstreets of his own city. Running the weights on your own infrastructure also has a security benefit: your sensitive data never leaves your own…

items.title: Anima, Bicameral
items.excerpt: Last Lightcone Commons grant round, two organizations stood out from the usual protest groups and think tanks. Both are brilliant and quixotic, and - I didn’t realize it at the time - have almost diametrically opposite agendas. Bicameral Labs is the brainchild of Erik Hoel; you might have read his Substack posts on aristocratic tutoring , the semantic apocalypse , or the gossip trap . In his day job, he’s a neuroscientist at Tufts who has spent his life trying to understand consciousness. I originally assumed Bicameral was his attempt to keep doing that under a fig leaf of alignment branding to see if he could attract some AI safety money - which, to be clear, I would be very sympathetic to. Then he bowled me over with the most original idea I’ve heard in months. Erik proposes qualiaphobic AI . He doesn’t know for sure if current neural networks are conscious, but he thinks he can build them in ways that ensure they won’t be, or at least minimize the chance. I am surprised by how confidently he thinks this: While we do not know how to build conscious AI, we know how to build non-conscious AI—or at least, AI that is hostile to current theories, and which would [only] be conscious according to the most extreme theories (such as those that are trivial or unfalsifiable), and which could only host phenomenologies so radically different they are impossible to conceive of (like those that could never underlie a self, qualify for personhood, or possess valence). items.title: Suggest Questions For The 2027 ACX/Metaculus Prediction Contest
items.excerpt: The ACX Prediction Contest is back for 2027, the fifth year Metaculus has hosted. There’s a $10,000 prize pool for the best forecasters, plus $3,000 for question suggesters. The ten people who contribute the most to the roughly 35 questions Metaculus selects will split the $3,000, with prizes from $150 to $700. Past question sets are in the 2025 and 2026 contests. This year is also an opportunity to see how far AI forecasting has come, as the best are now competitive with strong human forecasters. AI forecasting agents are welcome to enter and eligible for prizes, and Metaculus will post its own AI forecasts on every question. A good question suggestion has an objective answer that we’ll know by the end of 2027, with a source that settles it. “Will 2027 be especially hot?” is less good than “Will NASA’s GISTEMP data rank 2027 as the warmest year on record?” Suggest questions here by November 30. The contest will open in early 2027.

items.title: The AI Forecasting Agenda
items.excerpt: AI forecasters now equal or beat top human performance at traditional forecasting questions (eg ForecastBench , the Metaculus Cup ). These are usually specialized AIs with forecasting harnesses, created by forecasting startups (eg FutureSearch , Mantic , Preseen ), but foundation models like ChatGPT and Claude are only about six months behind the specialized models, so by the end of the year they’ll match top humans too. In the past, the options for getting top-human-level forecasts were slim and inconvenient. You could hire a team of superforecasters to work on the problem, but this would cost thousands of dollars and take weeks. Or you could check prediction markets (or Metaculus), but they only have a small sample of general-interest questions and are constantly trying to screw you over by gaming resolution criteria. The rise of AI forecasters solves these problems more cleanly and comprehensively than almost anyone thought possible just a year ago. The “science of forecasting”, which only recently felt like trying to pick the least-bad of various bad options, now faces tasks more like “what kind of magnifying glass should we use to inspect our giant novelty lottery check as we confirm that it’s real?” and “how do we spend our winnings?” Specifically: AI forecasters now equal or beat top human performance at traditional forecasting questions. items.title: Varieties Of Discourseposting
items.excerpt: I’m teaching at the Inkhaven blogging fellowship again this month. In my first class, I showed off terribly-written sentences and made the fellows analyze and improve them. Some were my own miscreations, some were Lyttle Lytton winners , and some came from the darkest abysses of the Internet. The audience’s favorite was overwrought description of women’s breasts from erotica (one person pointed out that my PDF reader’s Recent History tab helpfully displayed porn story titles while I presented on screen - why does a PDF reader even have a Recent History tab? - so I hope my humiliation helped educate you). But I hear that Naomi Kanakia ’s class was even spicier. She taught a course on “discourseposting”, which naturally descended into fiery discourse ( Naomi Kanakia, you are WRONG about Discourseposting!!! , Inkhaven Fight Club ). I didn’t get a chance to listen, so in the grand tradition of discourseposting, I’ll argue about it without having seen the source material. Sticking to our porn theme, and in the spirit of The Last Psychiatrist : one way to classify sex is through its external manifestations: positions, toys, fetishes. But another is through which psychological need it fulfills. The need to feel wanted. The need to feel valuable. The need to dominate. The need to lose yourself. Ask HN: Good ways to capture institutional knowledge?
items.excerpt: Successful companies institutionalize the knowledge of their employees; this leads to better continuity and faster on-boarding. Things like huge monorepos of useful code, internal tools, process manuals, etc. are example products of this. Young companies tend to depend on the dedication and talent of key individuals, and in maturation, must somehow make the jump to institutionalized knowledge (so that "if someone got hit by a bus" things are ok). What are some successful methods you have used or seen used to accomplish this transition? What are problems you faced (skeptics, opponents, etc.)? I am involved with an organization that is slowly growing, is about to lose key personnel, and is looking to prepare.

items.title: Inside the Fifa power struggle: Why Infantino is somehow still favourite?
items.excerpt: Uefa’s statements may have claimed “unanimous” support for Philippe Diallo as a Fifa presidential candidate from their members, but there isn’t quite such a united front in private. Some national associations, and other stakeholders, believe no one should have been entered so as to delegitimise the entire process. Instead, Diallo, the president of the French federation, may be facing up to a landslide defeat to Gianni Infantino.“He doesn’t stand a chance,” The Independent was told by one figure who ostensibly backed him. There is one big “if”. That may admittedly change for Diallo or respected Japanese candidate Kozo Tashima if a big calculation from Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin pays off. There is at least some possibility that their legal action, or four months of political pressure from the Democrats winning the House and scrutinising all of Donald Trump’s connections, may create problems for Infantino. Or, at least, voter doubt. items.title: MariTide Explained: Amgen's Once-Monthly GLP-1 Antibody Conjugate and Its Side Effects
items.excerpt: MariTide (maridebart cafraglutide, formerly AMG 133) is Amgen's investigational obesity drug: a fully human antibody that blocks the GIP receptor, linked to two GLP-1 agonist peptides, designed for once-monthly injection. This short covers how the dual mechanism works, what the Phase 1 trial and the 52-week Phase 2 trial in the New England Journal of Medicine showed on weight and blood sugar, where the Phase 3 MARITIME program stands, and what trials reported on side effects, from nausea and vomiting to GI dropouts and gallbladder events. We built an efficient manufacturing operation and grew the business to 50 million dollars in revenue. Then people actually stopped caring about masks. Fair enough. items.title: Context Scaling: A New Frontier of AI Scaling
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.33160v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many failures of deployed AI arise not from weak inference but from a mismatch between the state a task depends on and the context available when the system acts. Relevant user state, repository revisions, tool traces, sensor readings, or environment changes may be unavailable, distorted, or poorly selected. We call the effort to reduce this bottleneck context scaling. We frame a model as $P_\theta(d\mid c)$ within a system governed by three budgets: training $B_\theta$, decision-time $B_d$, and context-infrastructure $B_c$. Pretraining scaling invests in $\theta$; decision-time scaling searches, refines, or verifies decisions under supplied context; context scaling improves the system's capacity to acquire, represent, deliver, evaluate, and persist deployment state for model use. The three programs interact, but only $B_c$ targets what the system can make available before a decision. This view makes the model-infrastructure pair the unit of analysis. We define effective-context value as a task- and intervention-dependent attribution, separate deployment state from model-visible context, and identify availability, fidelity, selection, and utilization failures. We then organize current mechanisms through a five-operation context lifecycle and propose controlled budget interventions and utility-cost curves for evaluation. The resulting agenda centers on grounded reporting, interaction-data and full-cost infrastructure, and safety…

items.title: Constraint-Aware Test-Time Scoring for LLM and VLM Candidate Selection
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.33161v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When an LLM or VLM produces several candidate answers, picking the best one usually relies on the model's own confidence, a learned judge model, or a domain check. Each has a known weakness: an answer can be fluent but insecure, mathematically plausible but physically infeasible, or rated highly by a judge while quietly breaking a task requirement. We propose a scoring framework that combines a small set of hard checks every answer must pass with a wider set of softer checks whose scores are blended into one number per candidate. This adaptive scoring framework consists of three components: a drafting model that produces the candidates, a configuring model that selects and weights the checks for each task, and scoring models that rate properties no grounded tool can compute. We apply our proposed method to four tasks: writing code that is both correct and secure (CWEval), generating robot manipulation plans (LIBERO with added safety variants), passing competitive-programming hidden tests (LiveCodeBench), and answering questions from retrieved documents (HotpotQA). items.title: AutoformBench: A Lean Formalization Benchmark for Advanced Mathematics
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.33165v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI systems are increasingly capable of producing machine-checked Lean proofs of advanced mathematical results. Real mathematical formalization, however, is not isolated theorem proving: it requires building the definitions and intermediate lemmas that connect a result to a formal library. Existing evaluations often provide isolated theorem statements in settings where much of this supporting theory is already available in Mathlib. We introduce AutoformBench, a benchmark of 341 Lean 4 formalization tasks drawn from 24 advanced mathematical sources. Lean-experienced mathematicians formalized and audited each target statement, leaving the corresponding Lean proof to the evaluated agent. Each problem is embedded in a broader mathematical development: agents receive the informal proof but must translate it into Lean while constructing the missing definitions, intermediate lemmas, and supporting infrastructure. We compare the performance of frontier models on these problems. We find a largely shared difficulty frontier: success depends less on mathematical domain than on models' ability to construct missing formal infrastructure. Data and code at https://github.com/facebookresearch/autoformbench

items.title: General-Purpose Decision Models for AI Configuration Tuning
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.33190v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI configuration tuning searches for settings that improve the performance of AI systems under a limited budget. Existing tuners use different sampling and search policies, making the choice of decision strategy central to both tuning quality and cost. We investigate whether general-purpose decision models can guide tuning, using Jev as a deployed representative that returns structured choices and numeric scores across diverse tasks. To assess where it helps, we compare its use as an optimizer, performance predictor, and region guider against conventional methods and a large language model (LLM) on eight AI tuning tasks. Conventional optimizers attain rank 1 in six of eight comparisons. Similarly, established predictors outperform Jev in seven. Through region guidance, however, it finds configurations with lower perplexity than those selected by the native tuner, offering a quality gain when additional decision time and API fees are acceptable. These findings yield actionable recommendations on selecting the decision role, retaining conventional predictors, and balancing tuning quality against cost.

items.title: What, Who, and When: Structured Harm Assessment for Mental Health Safety via Short Reasoning
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.33263v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The growing use of large language models (LLMs) for mental health support raises important safety concerns. Existing guard models primarily identify categories of harmful content, often overlooking the context needed to determine an appropriate response. We introduce a clinically grounded taxonomy that characterizes harm along three dimensions: what the harm is, who is involved, and when it occurs. It further separates harm characterization from intervention decisions, thus enabling safety policies to be specified outside the model weights through explicit, clinician-curated instructions that can be updated and audited. We validate the taxonomy with expert clinicians and validate a panel of LLM judges to scale annotation. Relabeling public benchmarks in this taxonomy shows that they rarely contain harm directed at the user, which accounts for nearly half of the harm in real conversations. We then train MindGuard2, a 35B-A3B reasoning-based guard model using supervised fine-tuning on short reasoning traces followed by reinforcement learning with a reasoning-length penalty, to minimize inference overhead while preserving the benefits of reasoning. On two public benchmarks and real-world conversations, MindGuard2 achieves balanced accuracy comparable to the substantially larger GLM-5.3 at approximately 10x lower median latency, advancing the accuracy-latency Pareto frontier. items.title: How to choose the next safe step in application modernization
items.excerpt: A request to modernize an application often starts with a technology question: Which framework should replace the old one? Before you choose, find out what still works. Then collect evidence that can act as a regression net for that behavior and show where modernization is necessary. I used an evidence-first method on four public applications, from a small Node.js game to a large Java enterprise resource planning (ERP) application. Each needed a different treatment, but the way I collected evidence, chose the next experiment, and decided on possible proof points was repeatable. This post walks through that process so you can apply it to one application of your own. It also shows how to encode the procedure in a GitHub Copilot agent skill while keeping architectural judgment with the people responsible for the system. Build evidence before choosing a target The label on an application rarely tells you enough. “Java microservices” doesn’t tell you which Java Development Kit (JDK) runs in production, where that version is pinned, whether the tests execute, or which interfaces other systems depend on. “Legacy monolith” doesn’t tell you whether the business core is broken or whether one retired platform dependency prevents the application from starting. Before you recommend a change, build a small evidence inventory: Manifests, lockfiles, entry points, and deployable components Verified commands for installing, building, testing, packaging, and running Runtime pins in containers…

items.title: Maintainers don’t need more AI bug reports. They need fixes.
items.excerpt: AI has made finding potential vulnerabilities fast and cheap. Fixing them still takes human judgment, and in open source, that work falls to maintainers. Many are already flooded with AI-generated security findings, including duplicates and reports that aren’t vulnerabilities at all. Another raw scan doesn’t help them. Anyone pointing a new model at a project should ask its maintainers first and come with fixes, not just findings. Maintainers are under intense pressure from this flood of reports. As Christian Grobmeier, a maintainer of Log4j, has put it, the AI defending open source has to be better than the AI attacking it . AI shouldn’t add to maintainers’ workload. So, with maintainers, GitHub and Microsoft ran a pilot together: could AI help maintainers ship fixes instead of handing them more findings? GitHub and Microsoft are using Codename MDASH , Microsoft’s multi-model agentic scanning harness, to find and fix security vulnerabilities in widely used open source software, strengthening the foundation that much of the world’s code is built on. The process Our pilot had two goals: send only findings that matter, and never send a maintainer an unverified finding. Here’s how it worked: Find. Codename MDASH , an AI system from Microsoft Security, scanned each project using Microsoft’s MAI Cyber model and suggested fixes for what it found. Filter. items.title: Scientists say this pesticide needs a warning label for pollinators
items.excerpt: Of the many chemicals humans have invented to control agricultural pests, some of the most devious are called “ insect growth regulators .” As the name suggests, these compounds don’t kill insects directly; they alter their development so they can’t grow into healthy, reproducing adults. This makes insect growth regulators a remarkably useful tool for taming populations of insects like whiteflies and mealybugs, which can spread diseases and sap nutrients out of food crops. There’s just one problem: Farmers don’t want to regulate all insects in this way. Beneficial insects like honey bees risk getting caught in the crosshairs of these chemicals, to the detriment of farmers who need their pollination services to produce crops like pears and cherries. One insect growth regulator in particular has emerged as a potential issue for pollinators: buprofezin. Ongoing research out of Washington State University, or WSU, suggests that buprofezin may be hazardous to honey bees even at concentrations 10 times below those commonly found in pollen. A study published in 2024 connected the compound to “severe brood mortality.” At a meeting of the Washington State Beekeeping Association last month, WSU entomology professor Brandon Hopkins said buprofezin products should be sold with a pollinator warning — a break from current requirements of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, or EPA. Buprofezin “should carry the same bee-caution label that some of these more direct pesticides carry,”…
